title: Codebase Health
objective: Nobody had measured this codebase. Twenty-seven gates, 143 stories and a risk model governed how work arrives, and no number described the code the work produces: not coverage, not the unsafe surface, not the panic surface, not which document anyone reads. This epic measures first and then spends the measurement - hardening where the numbers say the risk is, and removing where they say a thing costs more attention than it catches. The centre of gravity is the code, not the process: the owner chose codebase health over adding method, and chose Rust first with a security pass on the frozen Python reference. Nothing is removed on taste: a removal arrives with its measurement, in its own reversible commit, and nothing guarding a Safety Invariant or the mutation boundary is removed for cost at all.

stories.title: The lint policy states the thesis the project already claims
stories.outcome: `[workspace.lints]` held one line - `unsafe_code = "forbid"` - so `cargo clippy -D warnings` ran the default set and nothing else. For a workspace whose argument is that a tool deleting files must never act on an unproven assumption, the default set says nothing about the two ways that fails: an unwrap that aborts mid-operation, and an unsafe block whose soundness argument was never written down. Measured first: 41 unsafe blocks against 30 SAFETY comments, and 13 panic sites in production code, six of them indexing strings that come from third-party provider manifests. The measurement also exposed a structural defect - Cargo's `[lints]` table is all-or-nothing, so cancellai-sealedfs, which must declare its own to lift `forbid`, was the one crate a workspace policy could never reach: every unsafe block in the repository sat in the only crate exempt from the rule about unsafe blocks.
acceptance_criteria: Every unsafe block in the workspace shall carry a written safety argument, enforced by the compiler rather than by review.
Production code shall not reach a panic through unwrap, indexing or slicing, on any tier-1 platform.
If a crate declares its own lint table, then a gate shall refuse any workspace lint it drops, because a local table replaces the workspace one rather than extending it.
Where a crate is exempt from a lint, the exemption shall be declared in that crate's source rather than in a manifest, so a reader of the code sees it.
If the policy is relaxed for tests, then the relaxation shall be explicit and shall not reach production code.
verification: Clippy with -D warnings passes on native, x86_64-pc-windows-gnu and x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu - seven of the eleven undocumented unsafe blocks only exist behind cfg(windows) and no single-platform run could see them.
The rewritten glob matcher is compared against a naive reference implementation over every pattern and input up to length four across an alphabet containing a multi-byte character.
The lint-policy gate is shown to fail when a lint is dropped from the sealedfs table, not merely to pass when it is present.
41 unsafe blocks and 41 SAFETY comments, asserted by a test independent of clippy so the property survives a lint being relaxed.

stories.title: Coverage may not fall where falling matters
stories.outcome: E27-S01 measured coverage for the first time and the headline was 94.54% of regions - a good number and the wrong one to act on, because an average hides its worst member and the worst member was cancellai-sealedfs at 92.54%, the crate holding every unsafe block and the mutation boundary. A ratchet records what each crate covers today and fails when a crate falls below it: nobody has to defend a threshold nobody can justify, and nothing can quietly get worse. Only the kernel ring plus policy and inventory are gated; the rest is recorded for visibility, because a rendering regression is a bug and not an authority failure.
acceptance_criteria: Region coverage per crate shall be recorded in version control and compared against a real measurement, not asserted.
If a gated crate covers less than its recorded floor, then the gate shall refuse and name both numbers.
A crate that improves shall not tighten its own floor silently: re-recording is an explicit, reviewable change.
If a gated crate is absent from the report, then the gate shall refuse rather than treat a crate that stopped building as passing.
Movement below a stated tolerance shall not be a regression, and the tolerance shall not be usable as a way through.
A crate that is a declared skeleton shall not be gated, so a correct zero is not reported as a crisis.
verification: The ratchet is shown failing on a lowered floor before it is shown passing.
The tolerance is tested from both sides: 0.4 below passes, 0.6 below fails.
The committed baseline covers every gated crate, asserted against the real file.
